People around the world are living longer. That's one of society's great achievements.
But it's also changing the economics of retirement. People may need their savings to last for decades,
while in many countries, more of the responsibility for funding those years
is shifting from governments and employers to individuals. At the same time, there is no single
global model for retirement, and different countries are tackling different pieces of the
challenge. One thing I think you can guarantee on retirement is that no two systems or two
countries look the same. There's three ways to help drive particular outcomes for retirement.
Help people save, how much you're saving. Two is how you translate those savings into
actual investments, and then three, taking those investments and turning that into a reliable
stream of income. So what can we learn from how different countries are responding? Which ideas
can travel across borders and which can't? And as retirement is rewired, do we need to think
differently about retirement itself? Not as a series of separate problems, but across the whole
portfolio and the whole lifetime. Welcome to The Bid, where we break down what's happening
in the markets and explore the forces changing the economy and finance. I'm Oscar Pulido.
Joining me today are Casey Maurer, head of U.S. Defined Contribution for BlackRock,
and Helen Lee Jones, EMEA head of Global Consultant Relations and Institutional Strategy.
Together, we'll look at the forces rewiring retirement around the world,
how different systems are adapting, and what those changes could mean for the future of retirement.
Helen and Casey, thank you for joining us on The Bid.
Thank you so much for having me here, Oscar. Great to be here.
Well, Helen, we're here in London. I'm visiting this week. I know this is where you're usually
based. And the topic today is retirement, which is something that everybody around the world is
thinking about and trying to prepare for. But it's important to take a step back and
acknowledge that the way in which people prepare might vary across different regions. It might look
different. I guess the first question I have for you, though, is why are we talking about
retirement so much today? What's changing that is bringing this topic forward in more conversations?
Well, that's a great question. And when you think about it around the world, what we're
seeing right now is that the retirement systems are being fundamentally rewired. Why is that?
Look at the world. It's completely different. The economic, demographic, and institutional
assumptions on which the old retirement systems were built no longer hold. So when you think about
it, the model was that in the 20th century, you'd work maybe for 35, 40 years, maybe for the same
employer, you'd retire perhaps for 10, maybe 15 years with good health, and then you receive
income from the state, your employer, or both. Now, what we're seeing is that people are living
much longer. And what we're seeing is that as those populations age and traditional defined
benefit pension systems are disappearing, governments are really facing a different
set of pressures, fiscal pressures, and individuals who now are increasingly
accountable for their own retirement. What we're seeing right now is really a structural shift
in the ecosystem. We're seeing a transfer of retirement responsibility, risk, and capital from
governments and employers all the way over to individuals. And that's really seeing a shift
in the market that we're here to talk about today. And one of the things that you mentioned as to
why we're talking about this is that individuals are living longer lives. This is good news,
but it comes with then a responsibility to help them think about how to save and invest and also
then spend in retirement. You talked about greater responsibility on that individual in terms of
managing those investments in retirement. And Casey, if I could come to you then for a second,
what does it mean when we're talking about individuals having to take
more of that responsibility? How is that changing what retirement systems are having to do
on behalf of these investors? First, Oscar, I think it forces us to rethink what success
actually looks like in retirement systems. As responsibility shifts more to individuals,
we're asking people to make pretty complex financial decisions at different points throughout
their life. And when we think about the phase in particular, for example, where someone is
approaching retirement, often this is where their own financial picture looks the most complex.
And kind of overnight, we're asking people to be part actuary, part investor, part financial planner.
And that is a tall order. One of those questions as well is how long do my savings need to last
for me? So not only is that a tough financial question to answer, it's also deeply personal.
When I think about what resonates with me with retirement, and one of the reasons I'm so passionate
about this work is when I was growing up, my parents knew that they would have the traditional
defined benefit pensions. One was a teacher, one was a military pilot, and what that gave them,
and really us as a family, was a sense of security about that time and their lives. And I think the
reality of this is it's less common nowadays. As responsibilities just to individuals, I don't
think this means that we just leave individuals to their own. I think there's a real role to play
for our policymakers, for the financial services industry, for employers to really help reduce
the complexity that individuals may face some of those questions that we talked about, and really
help solve for outcomes. If we think about retirement as the freedom to do what comes next,
then I think what success looks like is not the size of someone's retirement account, but actually
it's help in providing that certainty, that security to do just that, to be able to allow them to do
what's next. And Helen, Casey sits in the US, and maybe she's thinking about retirement through a
little bit more of a US lens. You're based here in the UK. You work a lot with savers and investors
across the broader European continent. What does retirement look like in parts of the world,
like the UK and Germany? Are there differences in those approaches? And is there anything that
is going on in those countries that we can learn and maybe apply in other parts of the world?
One thing I think you can guarantee on retirement is that no two systems or two countries look the
same. And really, when you look at the UK, it's going to fundamentally different place to Germany.
The UK system is really a market-based retirement system. It's got a range of different pension
savings options, whereas Germany is really a principally state-led pay-as-you-go system.
Maybe if we just bring that to life through some numbers, the OECD puts the UK pension
provider asset industry at almost $3 trillion. Compare that to Germany, and that's almost $300
billion, because our population sizes are pretty equivalent. In the UK, there's 70 million people.
In Germany, there's around 85 million people. But the pensions industry is not even a tenth
of the size of the UK. And so that really shows you how much of the pension provision is being
provided by the state rather than by the kind of commercial or pension savings industry.
But I think other really important piece to note is that they're in fundamentally different
starting points. We could look at the UK and say, wow, what a great success story. There's $3 trillion
of retirement assets. The UK has never really had a state-funded pensions industry. It's really
moved into the hands of the employer and the commercial sector since almost the 1950s. The
UK system has really advanced over many decades. And really what we're now seeing in the UK is
that system that has been in the hands of companies to provide for their employees through defined
benefit systems. It's now moving into defined contribution. They're almost in the kind of third
age of pension provision from state to fully corporate funded to now corporate provided in
terms of platform and defined contribution. But really the responsibilities falling to the
individual. And when you look at what's happened in the UK, regulation has really kind of triggered
a lot of that innovation. You go back to 2012 with the introduction of auto-enrollment where
employers really had to provide a mandatory pension saving system for their employees.
It's massively increased the amount of employees, the amount of savers into retirement systems to
almost 90 percent of eligible workers, which I think is a huge success of a regulatory change
here in the UK. Because Germany has had such great success in providing for pensioners in
retirement through a state-funded system, the impetus to change hasn't really been there.
But when we go back to the beginning of our conversation talking about those changing economic
and demographic shifts, that kind of shift towards needing to rethink the system I think
is increasing across many parts of Europe and around the world. But what we are seeing from
Germany is that there is a shift perhaps towards a little bit of the individual retirement
responsibility. There's going to be some reforms coming in at the end of this year where we'll see
the creation of a capital market-based retirement product, which will really put the
responsibility for investing into the hands of individuals even more so than it was before.
So when you think, what are we learning from these two markets? I think there are really
three things to take away. It's not a slow game, right? Retirement reform takes decades. This
plays out over a really long time frame. I think the second thing to really note is that
employer participation is really critical unlock to helping individuals save for their retirement.
It's much easier to help investors save if it's a default in your corporate pension plan
than having to convince millions of savers to go ahead and buy a financial investment product.
And then maybe the third story, and that's really related to the size of the UK system,
is that gaining access to capital markets and staying invested in capital markets over the
long horizon is really the critical part of having larger asset pools that can provide for
people in their retirement. Yeah, just on those last points, it sounds like the more you make it
convenient for people to save for retirement, the more you provide them access to capital markets,
that's beneficial to them. But there is that theme of the individual having to take responsibility,
perhaps the days of somebody's going to do it for you are starting to go away and
you have to do it more yourself. And Casey, perhaps to then come back to you,
where in the US, there's been a tremendous amount of success over the years with 401ks,
where individuals are saving and investing for themselves. They've done a great job of helping
people accumulate savings. But what is that next phase of the 401k look like as people are aging and
moving into retirement? And as you say, they want the freedom to do what's next. I think it builds
on actually some of what we just talked about. But the history of the 401k gives us a great
blueprint when we think about what could come next. One clear lesson is that plan design
really matters. And I think this is a timely conversation because in August, we just passed
the 20 year mark since the Pension Protection Act in the US. And what this did is helped
accelerate some really important innovations in the marketplace. So things like automatic
enrollment, investment defaults like target date funds. And so I think it's important to pause for
a minute there and actually say this is a success story. There are some really successful innovations
when we think about retirement systems. And oftentimes, when we're having this conversation
about retirement, we focus on the challenges. And that is really important. But I think the
opportunity now is to just build on that success. As you said, build on that accumulation system
and really think about how we can help people achieve particular outcomes. This is important
because there's still a gap. Our own research from read on retirement survey that we do every year
tells us that seven out of 10 American workers feel prepared for retirement. And that's pretty good.
But when we layer on our own research, what we actually see is that their own savings may translate
into just 50 to 60% of what they actually need. That's a shortfall of about half.
And that doesn't mean the 401k has fallen short. Let's be clear. It just means the evolution is
not over. And so I think we need to do two things. One is help people make those savings work harder
for them. What's exciting is there's a lot of innovation and creativity and value that the
industry is bringing to help people achieve this. And then the second is turning those hardworking
savings and investments into a reliable stream of income. And so I have a lot of optimism about this
because we're not starting from scratch and we don't need to reinvent the 401k. We just need to
finish the job. And one of the things that you mentioned in the US is this need to address
retirement income and help people also have a paycheck in retirement. There's another market
in the world very far from the US but similarly tackling this retirement income challenge which
is Australia. I'd love to hear a little bit more about what you see there and then maybe to contrast
that with a region of the world like Latin America where there it's more about expanding
access to markets. What are some of the observations in these different regions and what does it tell
us about the evolution of the retirement system around the world? Yeah, Oscar, I think one of the
most important lessons and Helen touched on this earlier is there's not a single model that works
everywhere. Different systems are tackling different parts of the retirement challenge.
And what we just talked about in the US, for example, is the innovations we've seen have made
it much easier for many working Americans but we're still working through how to translate
those savings into income. And then Australia, as you mentioned, is interesting because what we can
see is that they are further along in tackling income. They've built up huge retirement pools
of assets through superannuation funds and they're turning to their focus to how they can then
translate that to help support people through retirement, balancing things like longevity and
flexibility throughout. Mexico I think is another interesting example and what fascinates me is
they're tackling two sides of the equation. So one, increasing the amount that people save and then
two, the actual investments that are powering those savings and using things like target date
structures to help do that. I think stepping back what this is telling us is that there's three
ways just to simplify it to help drive particular outcomes for retirement. One is help people save,
how much you're saving. Two is how you translate those savings into actual investments and what's
powering that. And then three, taking those investments and turning that into the reliable
stream of income. And all three matter. The reality is no single market has the answer that works for
all. And one of the reasons I find the retirement story globally so interesting is that, like I
said, different systems are solving for different parts of it. But I do believe that good ideas
travel, countries can learn from each other. And at the same time, no market is exactly the same.
And finally, given that, we know it's very local at the same time. It's a very universal human
experience. And so I think the combination of learning across markets, remembering what we're
actually trying to solve for at the human level while coupling that with local implementation
is really, really critical. The good news is that there seems to be evolution going on around
the world. And that looks different in different regions. And like you said, a very local type of
solution depending on the population, the region that we're talking about, whether it's more
addressing retirement income or just expanding access to capital markets. And so Helen, it's
clear there are different ways to solve for this puzzle. As these retirement systems evolve though,
how does the industry need to adapt with them? And what does it mean to think about retirement
more holistically across the whole portfolio and the whole lifetime?
That is a great question, Oscar. And I just love those examples that Casey brought to live around
the innovation we're seeing in Australia and in Mexico and the US. And I think that diversity is
just a huge opportunity. And every time you see a market change, there's an opportunity for innovation.
And personally, I find that really exciting. And yes, I think pensions can be exciting. And I think
we're here on a mission to try and build excitement around the pension's opportunity for
individuals. Because joking aside, I think one of the challenges and opportunities for the industry
is that we've got to demystify a lot of the perceived complexity and anxiety around saving
for retirement. And when you look at the ecosystem as it stands today, it's really been built
for the same needs. It's just been advising corporates and governments to build pension plans
rather than individuals. So when you look at that ecosystem, and you mentioned the whole portfolio,
whole of life opportunity set, you could take that real institutional knowledge and convert it
into something that makes sense for the individual. So think about that in real terms. What does that
mean? It means financial panic, not only in your retirement, but to and through retirement. It also
means looking at things like new and creative investment products. So rather than having to
build complex asset liability, matching models and thinking about how to really ensure corporates
can provide for pensioners in their retirement, it's really about designing investment solutions
that do that for you. So think about investment products that provide income or investment products
that help draw down or spend your capital responsibly through a period of time in your
retirement. And then I think there are a whole host of other things that are happening around the
individual and around the industry, which probably are a little bit more behavioral in nature and
auto-enrollment, I think is a good example of that, where you're really seeing prompts and reducing
the friction of decision-making coming into play. So automatically putting employees into
pension-saving systems, automatically increasing your contributions to your pension as your earnings
increase, I think those types of systems and those types of evolutions in the market are going to be
some of the most important things that we'll see evolving over the next decades and centuries to
come, I'm sure. When I take a step back and really think about what's happening, we're really seeing
a blurring of the boundaries between institutional and individual investment ecosystems. And I think
in the past, you would have seen them as two very separate spaces. But that blurring, I think,
is really meaning that saving for your retirement is no longer a singularly defined moment. It's
almost moving from saving for retirement to just saving for a range of different life outcomes.
And I think increasingly that's going to be, as Casey mentioned, a really interconnected set of
choices that individuals are going to need to make over a whole lifetime. And what does that mean
for the ecosystem around it? For the financial services industry, it really means that we've
got to be thinking through how to help individuals make the best decisions at every step of that
journey along the way. And I think part of the blurring of those lines is historically we've
talked about defined benefit plans and defined contribution plans. And we've used some of that
terminology here in this discussion. And I think part of what's happening is that
some of those benefits of the pension, the defined benefit plan, professional management,
retirement income access to broader opportunities, I think some of that is coming to the defined
contribution space as well, Casey, if I understand correctly, where the individual still has ownership,
but is getting some of those benefits. Is that type of personal pension part of the next evolution
of retirement? I absolutely think so. When we think about the defined benefit plan and what
traditional pensions do so well, it is exactly what you just said. It's pooling the risk. It's
the professional investment management with a broad toolkit. It's that, in many cases, paycheck for
life. And then the DC plans bring different strengths. They have the ownership and portability
and flexibility. And that's really important. And so to me, the idea of the personal pension
is bringing some of those best features of the defined benefit plan into the modern retirement
system and the defined contribution space. And so this connects back to an idea I was talking
about earlier, this sense of security that my parents had. And so while this may look different
for many now and in the future, we shouldn't give up on trying to provide that same confidence.
And so I think that's what makes this idea so compelling. It's not about creating systems of
the past, but actually taking features of the defined benefit, things like guaranteed income,
things like private markets, where it makes sense to help power those investments,
and actually bringing them into the defined contribution space to preserving those things
that we all enjoy in that space, the flexibility ownership like we talked about. With this, I
think it's important and Helen touched on this a little bit as well. We have to remember that with
that increased sophistication or complexity, that all has to stay under the hood. We as an industry
have to absorb that complexity and can and are for the individual. I think that's really key as well.
And that's a great point. I think sometimes we talk about it a lot on the bid, which is financial
markets can be complex, and we're trying to demystify a lot of these topics. And retirement
can be complex if you want it to be complex, but the industry is really trying to simplify
and create more convenience for the end investor. Anytime we've done an episode on retirement,
listeners will know that I sometimes reference my own parents who are retired. And when I think
about what is it that gives me comfort is they have peace of mind. They took good steps in an era
before the system had evolved as much as it's evolving now. And so it sounds like from listening
to both of you that around the world, there's a lot of evolution going on in retirement systems
and is setting up a good foundation for more people to have this sort of peace of mind that
my parents seem to have right now. Helen and Casey, thank you so much for sharing this global
perspective on retirement. I'm sure we're going to be talking about this topic for many, many years
